lesson.title: Peaks in the Neighborhood: What Makes a Local Maximum
lesson.summary: A local maximum is a point where a function's value is at least as large as every nearby value, a neighborhood peak that does not have to be the single highest point of the whole function.
lesson.body:
A function has a local maximum at x = c if there is some open interval around c, however small, contained in the domain of f, on which f(c) is greater than or equal to f(x) for every x in that small interval. The word local is doing real work here: the comparison only has to hold nearby, not across the entire domain the way a global maximum requires. A function can have many local maxima, or none, regardless of whether it has a global maximum at all.

When f is differentiable at a local maximum c, there is a geometric signature worth noticing immediately: the tangent line at c is horizontal, meaning f'(c) = 0. This makes intuitive sense from the shape of a peak: the function has to stop rising just before c and start falling just after c, and the only way a smooth curve can switch from rising to falling without a jump is to pass through a moment of zero slope right at the top. This observation is the seed of an idea the chapter will name and formalize very soon.

Work through f(x) = x^3 - 3x, this time thought of as defined over all real numbers rather than restricted to a closed interval. Its derivative is f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3, which equals zero at x = -1 and x = 1. Focus on x = -1, and check the local maximum condition directly by comparing f(-1) to nearby values. First, f(-1) = (-1)^3 - 3(-1) = -1 + 3 = 2. Now test a point slightly to the left, x = -1.1: f(-1.1) = (-1.1)^3 - 3(-1.1) = -1.331 + 3.3 = 1.969, which is less than 2. Test a point slightly to the right, x = -0.9: f(-0.9) = (-0.9)^3 - 3(-0.9) = -0.729 + 2.7 = 1.971, also less than 2. Both nearby values are smaller than f(-1) = 2, matching the definition, so f does have a local maximum at x = -1, with local maximum value 2. As a quick check on the horizontal tangent observation, f'(-1) = 3(-1)^2 - 3 = 3 - 3 = 0, confirming the tangent line really is flat there.

It is important to see that this maximum is only local. Follow f(x) = x^3 - 3x out to very large positive x, and the x^3 term dominates, sending f(x) toward positive infinity, so no single output value can possibly be the largest one the function ever produces across all real numbers. The peak at x = -1 is a genuine peak in its own neighborhood, height 2, but somewhere far to the right the function eventually climbs past 2 and keeps going. That is precisely the gap between local and global that the earlier sections on the global maximum and global minimum were setting up.
